plain_english: It's not easy to fulfill your nature as a human being. What is a human being? A rational, mortal creature. Our rational mind is what separates us from wild beasts. It also separates us from sheep and similar animals. So be careful not to act like a wild beast. If you do, you've lost your humanity. You haven't kept your promise. Make sure you don't act like a sheep either. If you do, you've also lost what makes you human. What do we do when we act like sheep? We overeat. We're sexually reckless. We're impulsive, dirty, and thoughtless. When we do these things, we've sunk to the level of sheep. We've lost our rational mind. What about when we're argumentative, harmful, emotional, and violent? Then we've sunk to the level of wild beasts. Some of us become big wild beasts. Others become small, nasty little beasts. At that point, we might as well say, "Let a lion eat me." Either way, we've destroyed what it means to act like a human being.
original_excerpt: It is no common (easy) thing to do this only, to fulfil the promise of a man's nature. For what is a man? The answer is, A rational and mortal being. Then by the rational faculty from whom are we separated? From wild beasts. And from what others? From sheep and like animals. Take care then to do nothing like a wild beast; but if you do, you have lost the character of a man; you have not fulfilled your promise. See that you do nothing like a sheep; but if you do, in this case also the man is lost. What then do we do as sheep? When we act gluttonously, when we act lewdly, when we act rashly, filthily, inconsiderately, to what have we declined? To sheep. What have we lost? The rational faculty. When we act contentiously and harmfully and passionately and violently, to what have we declined? To wild beasts. Consequently some of us are great wild beasts, and others little beasts, of a bad disposition and small, whence we may say, Let me be eaten by a lion. But in all these ways the promise of a man acting as a man is destroyed.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: When does a complex statement work? When it does what it's supposed to do. A complex statement survives when all its parts are true. When does an either-or statement work? When it does what it promises. When do flutes, lyres, horses, and dogs stay in good condition? When they do what they're meant to do. So why be surprised that people work the same way? Each person improves and survives by doing the right actions. A carpenter gets better by doing carpentry. A grammarian gets better by doing grammar. But if someone gets used to writing bad grammar, his skill will definitely get worse and fall apart. Good actions preserve good people. Bad actions destroy them. Faithful actions preserve faithful people. The opposite actions destroy them. And the flip side is also true — opposite actions strengthen opposite traits. Shameless acts make shameless people stronger. Faithless acts make faithless people stronger. Harsh words make harsh people stronger. Anger makes angry people angrier. Taking more than you give makes greedy people greedier.
original_excerpt: For when is a conjunctive (complex) proposition maintained? When it fulfils what its nature promises; so that the preservation of a complex proposition is when it is a conjunction of truths. When is a disjunctive maintained? When it fulfils what it promises. When are flutes, a lyre, a horse, a dog, preserved? (When they severally keep their promise.) What is the wonder then if man also in like manner is preserved, and in like manner is lost? Each man is improved and preserved by corresponding acts, the carpenter by acts of carpentry, the grammarian by acts of grammar. But if a man accustoms himself to write ungrammatically, of necessity his art will be corrupted and destroyed. Thus modest actions preserve the modest man, and immodest actions destroy him; and actions of fidelity preserve the faithful man, and the contrary actions destroy him. And on the other hand contrary actions strengthen contrary characters: shamelessness strengthens the shameless man, faithlessness the faithless man, abusive words the abusive man, anger the man of an angry temper, and unequal receiving and giving make the avaricious man more avaricious.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: This is why philosophers tell us not to stop at just learning. We also need to study deeply, then practice what we've learned. We've spent years doing the wrong things. We've lived by bad ideas instead of true ones. If we don't start practicing the right ideas, we'll be nothing more than people who repeat what others have said. Right now, who among us can't give a proper speech about good and evil?
original_excerpt: For this reason philosophers admonish us not to be satisfied with learning only, but also to add study, and then practice. For we have long been accustomed to do contrary things, and we put in practice opinions which are contrary to true opinions. If then we shall not also put in practice right opinions, we shall be nothing more than the expositors of the opinions of others. For now who among us is not able to discourse according to the rules of art about good and evil things (in this fashion)?
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: Some things are good, some are bad, and some don't matter either way. The good things are virtues and anything that helps you be virtuous. The bad things are the opposite. The things that don't matter are wealth, health, and reputation. But then, if there's a loud noise while we're talking, or someone in the room laughs at us, we get upset. So where's your philosophy now? Where are all those ideas you were just discussing? They came from your mouth — just words. Why are you letting other people's reactions ruin what you've learned? Why are you treating the most important matters like you're rolling dice in a game?
original_excerpt: That of things some are good, and some are bad, and some are indifferent: the good then are virtues, and the things which participate in virtues; and the bad are the contrary; and the indifferent are wealth, health, reputation. Then, if in the midst of our talk there should happen some greater noise than usual, or some of those who are present should laugh at us, we are disturbed. Philosopher, where are the things which you were talking about? Whence did you produce and utter them? From the lips, and thence only. Why then do you corrupt the aids provided by others? Why do you treat the weightiest matters as if you were playing a game of dice?
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: There's a big difference between storing bread and wine in a warehouse and actually eating them. When you eat food, it gets digested and becomes part of you — your muscles, flesh, bones, blood, healthy skin, and healthy breathing. But stored food? Sure, you can grab it and show it off whenever you want. The only benefit you get is looking like you own something. So what's the difference between repeating these teachings and repeating the teachings of people who think completely differently?
original_excerpt: For it is one thing to lay up bread and wine as in a storehouse, and another thing to eat. That which has been eaten, is digested, distributed, and is become sinews, flesh, bones, blood, healthy color, healthy breath. Whatever is stored up, when you choose you can readily take and show it; but you have no other advantage from it except so far as to appear to possess it. For what is the difference between explaining these doctrines and those of men who have different opinions?
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: Go ahead and explain Epicurus's teachings by the proper methods. You might even explain them better than Epicurus did. So why call yourself a Stoic? Why lie to people? Why act like a Jew when you're really Greek? Don't you see what makes someone a Jew, a Syrian, or an Egyptian? When we see someone torn between two sides, we say, "This person isn't really a Jew — he's just pretending." But when someone truly takes on the feelings and beliefs of Jewish teaching and joins that way of life, then he really is a Jew. That's when we call him one.
original_excerpt: Sit down now and explain according to the rules of art the opinions of Epicurus, and perhaps you will explain his opinions in a more useful manner than Epicurus himself. Why then do you call yourself a Stoic? Why do you deceive the many? Why do you act the part of a Jew, when you are a Greek? Do you not see how (why) each is called a Jew, or a Syrian, or an Egyptian? and when we see a man inclining to two sides, we are accustomed to say, This man is not a Jew, but he acts as one. But when he has assumed the affects of one who has been imbued with Jewish doctrine and has adopted that sect, then he is in fact and he is named a Jew.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher
